topic: Unbounded LLM Inference OOMs Production GPU Nodes
postText:
A single user pasted a 40-page PDF into our medical summarization endpoint. The prompt fit in context length. The KV cache did not. GPU OOM. The pod restarted. Every clinician on that node lost their session mid-shift.

That was the day I stopped treating LLM inference like a normal web service.

Here is what production actually taught me about AI/ML architecture:

1. VRAM is not elastic. Unlike CPU or RAM on a VM, you cannot overcommit GPU memory. When the KV cache grows with sequence length and batch size, you hit a hard wall. The kernel does not swap. It dies.

2. Bound everything at the gateway. max_input_tokens, max_output_tokens, max_concurrent_requests. Reject early with a clear 4xx. Do not let the scheduler discover the limit for you.

3. Size your batch for the worst case, not the average. I reserve 30% VRAM headroom for cache spikes. Throughput looks lower on paper. Uptime looks much better in practice.

4. Admission control beats autoscaling for GPU. A new node takes minutes to warm. A queue with backpressure takes milliseconds. Shed load with 429 and let clients retry with jitter.

5. Separate training and serving paths completely. Training-serving skew is real, but so is resource contention. Different nodes, different quotas, different failure domains.

For healthcare IT, this matters more than most domains. A dropped inference request is not a lost page view. It is a clinician waiting on a summary while a patient waits on the clinician.

Question for the engineers here: when your GPU node is saturated, do you shed load, queue it, or scale out? What has actually held up under real traffic for you?

If this resonated, drop a comment with your own war story, hit Like so more builders see it, and Share it with your platform team. Architecture lessons are cheaper when shared.
